data.cultural_impact: The name Abeela holds a strong cultural significance in Islamic tradition. The bee is mentioned in the Qur'an several times as a symbol of industry and hard work. In Surah An-Nahl (16:68-69), Allah SWT says, "And your Lord revealed to the bee, saying: 'Take for yourself from the mountains, O bee, and from the trees and from the curtains which [belong to] the peoples. You shall construct dwellings from them in sculptured forms, and in each [form] find for yourselves a meal providing you with sustenance for a long time. Then see with what [various] designs and constructions He has made you. Indeed in that is a sign for the people who believe.' "
data.spiritual_significance: Abeela also holds spiritual significance in Islam. The bee is mentioned in Surah Al-Anfaal (8:41), where Allah SWT says, "If they deny you [O Muhammad ﷺ], so respond to their denial with one identical to it, and we will assist you with a brilliant victory." In Islamic tradition, the bee is seen as a metaphor for the community of Muslims who work together to create a peaceful and harmonious society, just as bees work together to build their hives and produce honey. The name Abeela is a reminder of the importance of cooperation and unity in the Muslim community, as well as the sweet reward that comes from working together towards a common goal.

historical_references.reference: Abeela was the name of a fortress city in Egypt which served as the capital of the Fatimid Caliphate from 969 to 1171 CE. The city was founded by Caliph Al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah and was named after his mother, Umm Al-Hassan Al-Sulayhiyya, who was also known as Shaghlawan Abeela. The city was strategically located at the mouth of the Nile Delta and was a center of Islamic learning and culture.
historical_references.context: Capital city of Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt

historical_references.reference: Abeela was also the name of a city in present-day Libya which was an important trading post during the Islamic period. The city was located on the coastal plain near modern-day Benghazi and was a center of the slave trade. The city was said to have been named after Abeela bint Rasheed, a Berber queen who ruled the region in the 10th century CE.
